text: The contract killers are serving prison sentences; they are signed out to do the work and signed back in when it is done. Erik Matti builds two hours of Manila crime around that arrangement, and around the symmetry of four men — two shooters, two agents of the law — who each treat what they do as a job with hours, wages and people at home waiting on the money. The chases are delivered in full. The attention, though, goes to the paperwork side of murder: who authorises the release, who is owed a favour, whose name never touches a document. Corruption here is not a revelation but a payroll, and the families of all four are on it whether they know it or not. Tagalog, 119 minutes, cut to the rhythm of men working against a deadline.

Two hours and twelve minutes is a long time to spend with a man who refuses to take a day off. Nawapol Thamrongrattanarit gives freelance work its full duration: the file that arrives near midnight, the client with one more revision, the body that begins filing complaints of its own. Comedy, romance and something more clinical share the frame, since the woman he is drawn to is the doctor he keeps having to see, and the appointment slot becomes the only fixed point in his week. Nothing here escalates the way a drama usually escalates. The question is simply whether a person can stop, and the film is patient enough to make that suspenseful. It keeps count of the hours the way its hero does, and lets the joke and the diagnosis sit in the same room.

The village's holy man looks at a newborn and gives him twenty years; everyone present has been counting ever since. Muzamil's father cannot live inside that arithmetic and leaves. His mother Sakina stays, keeps the boy close, and turns a death sentence into a regime of care so complete that it functions as confinement. Amjad Abu Alala is less concerned with whether the prophecy holds than with how a community arranges itself around believing it: how the boy is spoken to, what future anyone bothers to plan for him. Then Muzamil turns nineteen. In Arabic, 103 minutes, carrying Fribourg's Regard d'or, the film moves at the pace of people who think they already know the outcome and are waiting politely for it.

Twenty years in, the household runs on arrangements rather than conversation, and then news arrives that no arrangement can absorb. Maria Sødahl gives it 125 minutes, generous for a story with so few external events: rooms, appointments, children who must be told or not told, the quiet negotiation over who will manage which part of the day. The film is exact about the difference between a family and an administrative unit that shares an address. It is also unsentimental about how much of a long marriage consists of grievances shelved rather than settled, and how fast those resurface once the schedule breaks. The lead performance took the European Film Award for best actress. Norwegian, and closer to the truth of a bad week than to any tender idea of one.

Every January a priest throws a wooden cross into the river at Stip and the men of the town dive after it, since whoever surfaces with it is owed a year of good fortune. Petrunya jumps in on impulse and gets there first. The fury this provokes is the film's whole engine: not a supernatural rebuke, just men insisting on a rule nobody can quite locate in writing, and a woman declining to hand back what she won. Teona Strugar Mitevska keeps it to 100 minutes and to Macedonian, close on faces, with the deadpan of institutions trying to reverse an outcome without appearing to. The Lux Prize went to it, which suits a picture that is essentially an argument over custom conducted at room temperature by people who are still damp.

The bride is fourteen, and the household she enters already contains two wives, ranked in an order nobody has to explain to her. May learns her own position quickly: she is favoured, she is pregnant, and if the child is a son her place is secure. Ash Mayfair spends most of the 96 minutes at domestic scale — doorways, sleeping arrangements, women reading one another for information — in a house where the only currency is what a body produces. The film never forgets that its heroine is a child, or that almost everything she is learning arrives by observation rather than instruction. Then she sees something she was not meant to see. In Vietnamese, quiet nearly throughout, and far more curious about what the wives know of each other than about the man they share.

Two people bump into each other twice on the same Kutaisi street, arrange a date, and wake the next morning wearing faces neither of them will recognise. Alexandre Koberidze treats the curse the way a child treats a rule in a game: announced once, obeyed absolutely, then set aside so the film can attend to other things. Two and a half hours go largely to the town in summer — the river it sits on, football on every screen during the World Cup, passers-by filmed from a distance that turns them into weather. The romance waits. What holds the attention meanwhile is the camera's appetite for whatever happens to pass, with the fairy tale supplying just enough tension to keep it from drifting. Berlin's critics gave it the FIPRESCI prize. In Georgian, and slow on purpose.

Xolani takes leave from a factory job each year to spend a few weeks in the mountains, caring for boys recovering from circumcision. The camp is closed to women, and what happens there is not discussed outside it. That secrecy is the condition John Trengove works inside. Into it comes Kwanda, a teenager from Johannesburg, urban and defiant and quick to see what the men around him have agreed not to notice: that Xolani is in love with a man. Eighty-eight minutes, in Xhosa, with the physical discomfort of the camp left in the frame rather than composed away. The film understands that a code of manhood is taught less by instruction than by who may touch whom, and when, and in front of whom — and that the boys are learning the second lesson faster than the first.

Bread pays for the flat: Abla bakes at home in Casablanca and sells from the door, and her day runs on a fixed sequence of dough, school, housework. A pregnant stranger asking for work and a bed is therefore not a moral test but a disruption of the timetable, and Abla's first answer is no. Maryam Touzani stays inside that apartment for most of the 96 minutes and lets the negotiation happen through kitchen labour — hands in flour, a child hovering, two women who each need something and will not name it. Warda, who is eight, settles the question faster than either adult. The drama is the slow revision of a rule Abla made for reasons she can no longer quite defend, and the film is content to let it be revised at the speed of rising dough.

The surgery is finished before the film begins: Jade's face has been rebuilt, and she has to carry it back into a life that was organised around the old one. Sacha Polak starts where other versions of this story would end, with the scars healed enough to be permanent and everyone around Jade waiting for her to be all right. She is in her twenties with a small daughter, and the ordinary machinery of that age — friends, phones, going out, being looked at — keeps running whether or not she can rejoin it. The film is in English, 104 minutes, and it declines to make her a lesson in courage. Rotterdam's audience voted it their prize. Jade is not asking to be regarded kindly; she is asking to be let back in.

Hanging is a trade here, with procedures: measurements, forms, a senior man who has done it for decades and a younger one learning the sequence. Aiman transfers into the country's highest-security prison as a correctional officer and attaches himself to Rahim, the chief executioner, with an eagerness that has a second reason behind it. Boo Junfeng keeps the argument about capital punishment almost entirely out of the dialogue and puts it into the work instead — the rehearsals, the paperwork, the courtesy extended to men in cells, the pride of someone convinced he performs a necessary duty well. Ninety-six minutes in Malay, nearly all of it inside the walls. The unease comes from the apprenticeship: how fast a skill turns into a bond, and how badly Aiman wants the old man's approval.

Eighty minutes, divided into chapters, and for the first of them the organising principle is the men Hemel takes to bed. The pattern is the point. Sacha Polak lets it run a while before turning the film toward Gijs, Hemel's father — an auctioneer, well dressed, a man who has worked through a series of young girlfriends since his wife died. Between father and daughter there is an intimacy with no proper name and no line either of them has troubled to draw. Then Gijs meets Sophie, who is charming, and who appears to be staying. The film's virtue is that it declines to diagnose: Hemel is not a case study, her father is not on trial, and the plainness of the telling — daylight, ordinary rooms, unembarrassed talk about sex — leaves the discomfort where it was found.

Paulina gives up a promising legal career in Buenos Aires to teach at a suburban school under an inclusion programme, and her father, a judge, takes the decision as a personal defeat. Two weeks in, she is attacked by a group of men near the neighbourhood where she works. Then she returns to the classroom. Santiago Mitre builds everything after that on her refusal to be moved, and the pressure comes less from the attackers than from the people who love her and want her to be sensible — the father above all, reasonable and relentless. Her conviction is not comforting. It is stubbornness with a political argument fastened to it, and across 103 minutes Mitre turns it around in the light, in Spanish, arriving nowhere restful.

The season of the title lasts weeks, and so does everything else on Ling's schedule: fertility treatment fitted around a timetable, an infirm father-in-law at home who has to be lifted and fed, and a remedial Chinese class her students treat as a penalty. One of them, Kok Wei Lun, keeps turning up for the extra tutoring. Anthony Chen lets the attachment grow slowly and without menace, which is what makes it difficult: the boy's crush is entirely ordinary, the teacher's exhaustion is total, and both occupy the same small rooms. Care is the subject — who needs it, who is assumed to supply it, and how little of it comes back to a woman running a household and a classroom at once. In Chinese, 103 minutes, damp all the way through.
